claims.text: TC4 is a Ti6Al4V alloy with an alpha-plus-beta dual-phase microstructure.
Untreated TC4 has low hardness and inadequate friction and wear performance under extreme-service, high-contact-stress conditions.
The proposed intervention deposits a less-than-50-micrometer Inconel 718 transition layer and then an approximately 300-micrometer (TiAl)89-Cu5-Ni6 layer by pulsed laser cladding.
The Inconel 718 transition layer will act as a thermal-expansion and bonding buffer between TC4 and the HEA coating.
Cladding will be performed in argon at around 1500 W and 600 mm/s with optimized pulse duration.
The optimized process will achieve a cooling rate of at least 10^3 K/s while minimizing diffusion, avoiding brittle intermetallic formation, and preserving the substrate's dual-phase structure.
The dual-layer process will produce a graded, defect-free interface with excellent metallurgical bonding.
The HEA top layer will develop a fine dendritic/eutectic microstructure.
Ni dissolved in the Ti(Al,Cu)2 phase produces solid-solution strengthening.
Inconel 718 buffers thermal stress through thermal-expansion matching and improves interfacial bonding.
Rapid solidification during laser cladding refines the HEA microstructure.
Ni stabilizes the Ti(Al,Cu)2 phase against intermetallic formation.
The coating will minimize residual stress relative to conventional laser-cladded coatings.
The modified surface will have approximately twice the microhardness of untreated TC4.
The modified surface will have a friction coefficient 40-50% lower than untreated TC4.
The coating will significantly improve wear resistance under high-contact-stress conditions.
The surface treatment will preserve TC4's low density and biocompatibility.
Keeping the Inconel 718 layer below 50 micrometers and the HEA layer near 300 micrometers is necessary for acceptable performance.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats intermetallic formation as something the process should avoid and as a possible falsifier, yet its proposed strengthening mechanism relies on the Ti(Al,Cu)2 phase, and the cited same-system evidence identifies Ti3Al and Ti(Al,Cu)2 as constituent intermetallic phases. The intended distinction between acceptable designed phases and deleterious intermetallics is not stated.
